title: Decision: blue-green deploys for the order intake service
gist: Decision record adopting blue-green deploys for the order intake service, with a hold window bounded by the worst consumer lag on record.
retrieval_text:
# Decision: blue-green deploys for the order intake service

## Context

Rolling deploys restart consumers one at a time, which is fine when the queue is shallow and unsafe when it is not.
The intake queue is not reliably shallow.

## Decision

We will deploy the order intake service blue-green, and we will hold the previous colour until the new one has drained the queue below its pre-deploy depth.

## Consequences

The hold period is bounded by the worst consumer lag we have measured, which is forty minutes.
Holding both colours doubles the consumer footprint for the length of the window.

## Alternatives considered

Canary deploys were rejected because a partial rollout leaves two retry policies in force at once.

title: Incident: checkout timeouts during the evening peak
gist: Incident writeup for the evening-peak checkout timeouts, tracing the outage to a retry storm that saturated the intake queue's consumer group.
retrieval_text:
# Incident: checkout timeouts during the evening peak

## Summary

Checkout requests timed out for thirty-one minutes during the evening peak.
No orders were lost; every submission that reached the queue was eventually processed.

## How it failed

The payments provider began returning 503s to every authorisation call.
Every failed message re-entered the intake queue on backoff, and because backoff is scheduled per message the queue consumer group spent the whole window redelivering work it could not complete.
Consumer lag rose to roughly forty minutes before the provider recovered.

## Contributing factors

The dead-letter threshold of five attempts was too high for an outage of this shape.
A message that will never succeed still burns five consumer slots before it is parked.

## What we changed

We shortened the dead-letter threshold to three attempts.
We added a circuit breaker in front of the payments client so that a provider outage stops producing new work.

## Timeline

The provider recovered on its own and no rollback was performed during this incident.

title: Runbook: draining an intake queue backlog
gist: Runbook for draining a backlog on the intake queue, covering when to scale the consumer group and when to park messages by hand.
retrieval_text:
# Runbook: draining an intake queue backlog

## When to use this

Use this when consumer lag on the intake queue exceeds ten minutes and is still climbing.

## Steps

1. Check the payments provider status page before scaling anything.
2. Scale the consumer group to twice its steady-state size.
3. If lag keeps climbing, park the oldest thousand messages in the dead-letter queue by hand.

## After

File an incident note even when nothing was lost.
A backlog that drains itself is still a signal about the retry policy.

title: Order intake service — design note
gist: Design note for the order intake service, covering the queue consumer, its retry policy, and the idempotency key that makes replays safe.
retrieval_text:
# Order intake service — design note

## Scope

The order intake service accepts checkout submissions over HTTP and hands each one to a durable queue.
Everything downstream of the queue is asynchronous.

## Queue consumer

A single consumer group drains the intake queue.
Each message carries an idempotency key derived from the cart id and the submission timestamp, so a replayed message is a no-op rather than a duplicate order.

## Retry policy

Failed messages are retried with exponential backoff, starting at two seconds and doubling to a ceiling of sixty seconds.
After five attempts the message moves to the dead-letter queue and pages the on-call engineer.

## Known limits

Backoff is scheduled per message rather than per consumer, so a broad downstream outage produces a retry storm rather than a clean pause.
Nothing in this design caps the total redelivery rate across the consumer group.
